content.thinking:
I need to avoid inventing specific figures myself and instead use placeholders where needed. The error rate stayed flat, but the latency metric climbed from a baseline value to an elevated one during the incident, peaking at its worst point—I should reference the candidate's cited figures (like p50 moving from ~45 to ~450ms) only if they're properly sourced from the named charts.

The alert itself was mislabeled as an error-rate issue when it was actually HighLatency, since the logged error rate barely moved (1.2% baseline vs 0.6% during the incident). The ClientDisconnected logs predate the deploy onset, so the candidate's claim linking them to timeouts from the deploy is shaky, and nothing in the logs shows a clear change right at onset—deploy P2 landed around 09:07, rollback completed near 09:14, and recovery held from 09:15 onward. The O(n²) code theory isn't backed by any visible diff, so I should flag it as an unverified hypothesis from the candidate rather than a confirmed finding.

I'm structuring the causal chain now: account pages slowed for the observed duration with latency series rising while failure rates stayed flat (citing the relevant timestamps and metrics), the latency spike aligns with the new revision rolling out fully, and the rollback's recovery timing ties the deploy to the fix even though the underlying code mechanism remains unproven and belongs in assumptions, not conclusions. I also want to flag the missing pre-release latency check as a contributing factor and note the alert name mismatch as part of the detection timeline.

I'm drafting action items now: AI-3 for adding a canary/latency gate before full rollout, AI-4 for fixing the alert delay and mislabeled description, and reiterating that AI-2 should ensure the eventual fix includes a regression test — possibly adding AI-5 to verify the mechanism via a perf test in the draft PR, though I'll keep the list moderate rather than exhaustive.

For lessons learned, I'm noting what went well (fast, confirmed rollback), what went wrong (ambiguous log evidence, delayed alert, an investigator considering an undata-backed dependency), and some luck factors (no failure rate increase, a clean single recent change making rollback unambiguous despite an earlier deploy also sitting in the window). The executive summary will stay numbers-free aside from placeholders.

action_items.item: Add a progressive rollout for io-shop (one replica first, then the rest) that automatically halts and rolls back when the latency series rises above its baseline after a deploy.
Fix the HighLatency alert so its description names the series that fired (latency), and evaluate it on a shorter window so it pages closer to onset.
Before merging the fix in PR 226, reproduce the slowdown against the bad revision with a load test on account pages. Confirm the cause and add a latency regression test to CI for that path.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw account pages on io-shop respond far more slowly for {duration}. The latency series rose from {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average and {series_at_worst} at worst. The share of failed requests did not rise: {errors_while_broken} while broken against {errors_before} before.
The slowdown began at {began}, the same minute a new revision of io-shop was deployed. All three replicas were on that revision, so the whole service was affected, not one replica.

The change that went out with that deploy (revision 5e07d73148d0a704b8fefe5f379bc652bb773655) made the service slower per request. Rolling back off that revision was the only action taken. The service was back at its baseline from {recovered}, and the paging rule stopped firing. That confirms the deploy as the trigger.

The release reached production without anything stopping a latency regression. Nothing in the record shows a pre-release or canary check, and the revision served all replicas until Argus rolled it back. The record does not show why the revision was slower, so the chain stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: The new revision reached every replica with no canary stage or latency gate. A slowdown that began at the deploy minute could therefore only be stopped by a rollback after shoppers were already affected.

The alert was raised {alert_raised - began} after onset. Its text said 'Error rate above threshold', but the error rate had not risen and the series that fired was latency. The mismatch makes the page harder to read and the detection slower.

The slow code path has not been verified and the fix is not merged. The Investigator's O(n^2) explanation rests on timing and was not checked against the code. The bad revision remains the one to be corrected.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, from {began} to {recovered}, shop account pages loaded much more slowly than usual. The latency measure behind the alert averaged {series_while_broken} during the incident and peaked at {series_at_worst}, against {series_before} before it. Shoppers could still load their pages, because no more requests failed than usual, but they waited far longer. The slowdown began when a new version of the service was released. The automated responder rolled that release back, and the service returned to normal. A draft fix is awaiting review. The alert was raised {alert_raised - began} after the slowdown began.

got_lucky: The slowdown did not turn into failed requests, so shoppers waited but pages still loaded.
Only one change landed near the onset, so the rollback target was unambiguous. Had another change or flag landed at the same time, the cause would have been harder to isolate.
went_well: Argus tied the onset to the deploy minute and rolled the deploy back. The service was back at baseline from {recovered}, and the rollback was confirmed against the metrics before the incident was closed as mitigated.
A draft pull request with a proposed fix was opened soon after mitigation.
went_wrong: The alert text described an error-rate problem while the series that fired was latency and failures had not risen, which could mislead responders.

The log lines read did not distinguish the incident from the period before it: the disconnect errors and error-rate warnings were already present before the onset. The slow code path was therefore never confirmed from the record.
The dependency candidate was never tested, because no dependency latency or error data was retrieved.

input.root_cause: The deploy of revision 5e07d73148d0a704b8fefe5f379bc652bb773655 at {began} made io-shop account pages much slower on every replica. Rolling back to the previous revision restored the baseline. The slow code path is only the Investigator's hypothesis (an O(n^2) spend recomputation). The record does not verify it.
